pos: n. (town of Suffolk; Rowland Taylor's parish, who was burnt outside it in 1555)
etymology: From Old English Hāðlēah, the heath clearing; hāð, heath, and lēah, a clearing.
biblical_def: Hadleigh was one of the first English towns to receive the gospel and it kept it. A prosperous Suffolk cloth town, it had heard Thomas Bilney preach, and from 1544 its rector was Rowland Taylor, a Cambridge man and chaplain to Cranmer, who taught and visited there for ten years. Under Mary he was summoned to London, and when friends urged him to flee as others had done he refused on the ground that he would not leave his people to a wolf; he was condemned and sent back into Suffolk to be burnt on Aldham Common, within sight of Hadleigh, on 9 February 1555, the same day Hooper died at Gloucester. The townspeople lined the road. The dictionary records the town because Taylor's reason for staying is the Lord's own definition of the office: “I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (Joh 10:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a shepherd as one who tends sheep, and figuratively a pastor; a rector as a clergyman who has the charge of a parish; and to spend as to expend, to lay out, to consume.
webster_full: SHEPHERD, n. A man employed in tending, feeding and guarding sheep; figuratively, a pastor or minister of the gospel.
RECTOR, n. [L. rector.] A ruler or governor; a clergyman who has the charge and cure of a parish.
SPEND, v.t. To expend; to lay out; to consume; to waste; to squander.
COURSE, n. [L. cursus.] A running; a race; the ground run over; progress; the track or line of motion.
scriptures: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.

But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
And I will very gladly spend and be spent for you; though the more abundantly I love you, the less I be loved.
He saith to him again the second time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my sheep.
corruption_summary: Rowland Taylor's Suffolk parish; he refused to flee under Mary and was burnt on Aldham Common within sight of the town in February 1555.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The question Taylor faced is live and not simple: whether a minister under threat should flee and preserve himself for later service, as Knox, Jewel and Cox did, or stay with his congregation. The dictionary does not condemn the exiles, who gave the English church its later leadership and its Geneva Bible. It records Taylor because somebody has to stay, and because the men who fled were themselves clear that the shepherd who stays has chosen the harder and more honourable part.

The principle to recover is that the pastoral office is a spending of the man for the people, and that his own safety is not the governing consideration. Paul will not weigh his life in the balance at all, saying “neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy” (Act 20:24). To a congregation that loved him less than he loved it he still says, “I will very gladly spend and be spent for you” (2Co 12:15). And the commission restored to Peter is a single word repeated: “Feed my sheep” (Joh 21:16).

“Feed my sheep” (Joh 21:16) — burnt on Aldham Common, 9 February 1555.

pos: n. (town of Oxfordshire; a byword for Puritanism, and William Whately's pulpit for thirty years)
etymology: From Old English Banneburh, the stronghold of Banna; burh, a fortified place.
biblical_def: Banbury was so thoroughly Puritan that Jacobean playwrights used its name as a joke, and the man who made it so was William Whately, vicar from 1610 until his death in 1639, called the roaring boy of Banbury for the force of his preaching. His lasting books were on the household: A Bride-Bush, a treatise on marriage, and A Care-Cloth, on its troubles, which went through several editions and are among the fullest Puritan treatments of the duties of husband and wife. He pressed the headship of the husband and the reverence of the wife, and pressed just as hard the husband's duty to love, provide and not embitter. The dictionary records the town because the Puritan recovery of the household is one of the Reformation's most practical fruits, and its charter is a single verse: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it” (Eph 5:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines marriage as the act of uniting a man and woman for life; reverence as fear mingled with respect and esteem; and bitter as sharp, severe, cruel in speech or temper.
webster_full: MARRIAGE, n. The act of uniting a man and woman for life; wedlock; the legal union of a man and woman for life.
REVERENCE, n. [L. reverentia.] Fear mingled with respect and esteem; veneration; honor due to a superior.
BITTER, adj. Sharp; cruel; severe; reproachful; sarcastic, as bitter words.
HOUSEHOLD, n. Those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family; a family living together.
scriptures: Eph 5:25
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
Eph 5:33
Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself; and the wife see that she reverence her husband.

Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered.
Col 3:19
Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them.
corruption_summary: A Jacobean byword for Puritanism; William Whately, the roaring boy of Banbury, preached there thirty years and wrote on marriage.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the modern denial of created order in marriage, which rewrites headship as an interchangeable partnership or as a cultural accident of the first century, and which the dictionary rejects as a corruption of Genesis 2 and Ephesians 5. The answering corruption is the one Whately himself preached against week by week: headship claimed without the love and the self-giving that define it, so that a husband asserts an authority he has not earned by sacrifice. Both errors leave the wife unloved; only one of them admits it.

The principle to recover is the whole of the apostolic household order, each duty stated as given. Paul sets the two side by side without softening either: “let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself; and the wife see that she reverence her husband” (Eph 5:33). Peter makes the husband's understanding of his wife a condition of his own prayers being heard, bidding him “dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife” (1Pe 3:7). And Paul forbids the commonest failure in one clause: “Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them” (Col 3:19).

pos: n. (town of Northamptonshire; where the Baptist Missionary Society was founded on 2 October 1792)
etymology: From Old English Cytringan, the people of Cytra; a tribal settlement name.
biblical_def: Kettering is where modern Protestant missions acquired an organisation. On 2 October 1792, in the back parlour of a widow named Beeby Wallis, twelve Baptist ministers of the Northamptonshire Association met after a day of preaching and resolved to form a society for propagating the gospel among the heathen; Andrew Fuller was its secretary, and the subscription they raised that evening came to thirteen pounds, two shillings and sixpence. William Carey, whose Enquiry had argued the case and whose sermon had pressed it, sailed for Bengal the next year and spent forty years there, producing translations of the Scriptures in Bengali, Sanskrit, Marathi and other tongues. The dictionary records the town because the enterprise rested on a plain reading of a command the church had argued its way around for two centuries: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations” (Mat 28:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mission as the sending of persons to propagate religion; a subscription as the sum subscribed, money promised by setting one's name; and to enlarge as to make greater in extent.
webster_full: MISSION, n. [L. missio.] A sending or being sent, usually by authority, to propagate religion, or to enlighten the heathen; persons sent, with their train.
SUBSCRIPTION, n. The sum subscribed or promised to be contributed; the act of attesting by writing one's name.
ENLARGE, v.t. To make greater in quantity or dimensions; to extend in limits; to amplify.
HEATHEN, n. A pagan; a gentile; one who worships false gods, and is not acquainted with the true God.
scriptures: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen.
Isa 54:2
Enlarge the place of thy tent, and let them stretch forth the curtains of thine habitations: spare not, lengthen thy cords, and strengthen thy stakes;
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
corruption_summary: Where twelve Baptist ministers founded the Baptist Missionary Society in a back parlour in October 1792, raising thirteen pounds two shillings and sixpence.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Carey had to argue against came from inside his own circle: a hyper-Calvinism which held that since the gospel call is effectual only to the elect, and since the apostolic commission lapsed with the apostles, there was no warrant to urge Christ on the heathen or to organise for the purpose. The dictionary is thoroughly Calvinistic and names this as a corruption of Calvinism, not an application of it; sovereign election is the ground of missionary confidence, since it guarantees that the preaching will not be in vain. The modern corruption runs the other way, replacing the message with development work and the call to repentance with a programme.

The principle to recover is the standing force of the commission and the promise attached to it. Christ's own words bind the whole period until His return, “and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world” (Mat 28:20). Isaiah commands an expectation to match it: “Enlarge the place of thy tent” (Isa 54:2), and spare not. And Paul puts the sending first in the chain, asking “how shall they preach, except they be sent?” (Rom 10:15).

“how shall they preach, except they be sent?” (Rom 10:15) — Carey sailed for Bengal the next year.

pos: n. (town of Leicestershire; a centre of Puritan preaching under the patronage of the Earl of Huntingdon)
etymology: From Old English Æsceby, the ash-tree farm, with the Norman family name la Zouche.
biblical_def: Ashby-de-la-Zouch was a preaching town made by a patron. Henry Hastings, third Earl of Huntingdon, a convinced Protestant nobleman, used his wealth and his appointments to plant able preachers across the midlands, and at Ashby he settled Anthony Gilby, a Marian exile from Geneva who had helped with the Geneva Bible, as lecturer; John Brinsley the elder kept the grammar school. The town became a resort for ministers and for the exercises called prophesyings, in which preachers met to expound a text in turn before one another and the people, a practice Elizabeth suppressed and the Puritans valued as the best training a preacher could have. The dictionary records the town because the maintenance of preaching is not charity but obligation: “Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel” (1Co 9:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a lecturer as a preacher in a church hired by the parish to assist the rector; to communicate as to impart, to share; and double honour as a twofold regard, including maintenance.
webster_full: LECTURER, n. One who reads or pronounces lectures; a preacher in a church, hired by the parish to assist the rector or vicar.
COMMUNICATE, v.t. To impart; to give to another; to share with another; to bestow.
PATRON, n. [L. patronus.] A protector; a supporter; one who countenances or supports; one who has the gift of a benefice.
HONOR, n. [L. honor.] Esteem due or paid to worth; high estimation; also, reward, that which confers distinction.
scriptures: Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel.
Gal 6:6
Let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things.
Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine.
Php 4:15
Now ye Philippians know also, that in the beginning of the gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church communicated with me as concerning giving and receiving, but ye only.
corruption_summary: Anthony Gilby's lectureship under the Earl of Huntingdon; a resort for Puritan preachers and for the prophesyings Elizabeth suppressed.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the starving of the ministry, which takes two forms and the dictionary rejects both. The first is an establishment which holds the endowments and does not require preaching of the men who draw them, which is what made the Elizabethan lectureships necessary: a parish could have a rector who never preached and had to pay a second man to do it. The second is the modern expectation that the minister should keep himself, or should be paid so little that he must, which Paul treats as a defiance of a direct ordinance of the Lord.

The principle to recover is that those taught owe maintenance to those who teach, by command and not by generosity. Paul states the duty from the hearer's side: “Let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things” (Gal 6:6). He singles out the preaching elders for the larger share, that those who rule well be “counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine” (1Ti 5:17). And he remembers by name the one church that did it when no other would (Php 4:15).

pos: n. (town of Essex; the English town with the heaviest concentration of Marian martyrs)
etymology: From Old English Colneceaster, the Roman fort on the Colne; ceaster, a walled town.
biblical_def: Colchester lost more of its people to the Marian fires than any other English town of its size. An Essex cloth town with a long Lollard inheritance and close trade with the Low Countries, it had read Tyndale early and in numbers, and between 1555 and 1558 some two dozen of its inhabitants and of the villages around it were burnt, several in batches, at the castle ditch and in the town. They were weavers, tanners, labourers, a few women, one blind man; the records in Foxe give their trades and their answers under examination, and the answers turn repeatedly on the Supper and on the authority of Scripture. The dictionary records the town because the great multitude John is shown is made of exactly such people: “These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev 7:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tribulation as severe affliction, distresses of life; a robe as an outer garment, a gown of state; and precious as of great price, highly valued.
webster_full: TRIBULATION, n. [L. tribulatio.] Severe affliction; distresses of life; vexations; in Scripture, trouble endured for the gospel.
ROBE, n. [Fr. robe.] A kind of gown or long loose garment worn over other dress, particularly by persons in elevated stations.
PRECIOUS, adj. [L. pretiosus.] Of great price; costly; of great value or worth; highly esteemed.
EXAMINATION, n. [L. examinatio.] The act of examining; a careful inquiry; interrogation of a witness or accused person.
scriptures: Rev 7:14
And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.
Rev 7:17
For the Lamb which is in the midst of the throne shall feed them, and shall lead them unto living fountains of waters: and God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes.
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
Act 7:59
And they stoned Stephen, calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.
corruption_summary: The Essex cloth town that lost some two dozen of its people to the Marian fires between 1555 and 1558.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the Marian persecution and the doctrine that drove it: the judgment that a weaver who denied transubstantiation was a heretic whose body should be burnt, pronounced by bishops who had themselves subscribed the Edwardian settlement a few years before. The dictionary notes that the English Reformation also killed, under Henry and later under Elizabeth, and that this does not excuse Mary's reign; the principle the dictionary rejects is the principle both used, that the magistrate's sword may settle a confession.

The principle to recover is the honour God puts on the deaths of obscure believers. The psalmist states it flatly: “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints” (Psa 116:15). The martyrs in John's vision are promised a shepherd and an end of grief, since “the Lamb which is in the midst of the throne shall feed them” (Rev 7:17), and God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes. And the first of them set the words that the Colchester records show several of them using: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Act 7:59).

pos: n. (abbey town of Suffolk; where two men were hanged in 1583 for distributing Robert Browne's separatist books)
etymology: From Old English byrig, a fortified place, with the name of Edmund, the East Anglian king buried there.
biblical_def: Bury St Edmunds held one of the greatest English abbeys and, after its dissolution, one of the sharpest tests of the Elizabethan settlement. Robert Browne, the first Englishman to argue in print for churches gathered by voluntary covenant and independent of the bishops, had his books circulated in Suffolk; at the Bury assizes in June 1583 two men, John Copping and Elias Thacker, were tried for distributing them and hanged, their copies burnt before them. Browne himself was repeatedly imprisoned and eventually conformed. The monk Richard Bayfield, burnt in 1531 for importing Tyndale's books, had been of the abbey here. The dictionary records the town because the question Browne raised is a real one and the answer Gamaliel gave is the right procedure: “Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought” (Act 5:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a separatist as one who withdraws from an established church; to assemble as to come together, to meet; and to overthrow as to demolish, to defeat, to destroy.
webster_full: SEPARATIST, n. One that withdraws from a church, or rather from an established church, to which he has belonged; a dissenter.
ASSEMBLE, v.i. To meet or come together; to convene, as a number of individuals.
OVERTHROW, v.t. To turn upside down; to demolish; to destroy; to defeat; to conquer.
COVENANT, n. [L. convenio.] A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract.
scriptures: Act 5:38
And now I say unto you, Refrain from these men, and let them alone: for if this counsel or this work be of men, it will come to nought:
Act 5:39
But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it; lest haply ye be found even to fight against God.
But he answered and said, Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
corruption_summary: Two men hanged at the Bury assizes in June 1583 for distributing Robert Browne's separatist books, and their copies burnt before them.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the hanging. Whatever the merits of Browne's ecclesiology, two men died for carrying books in a Protestant kingdom, which is the same principle Mary's bishops used and the dictionary rejects in both hands. On the doctrine itself the dictionary is not neutral: it holds the congregational governance of the local church, which is Browne's substantial point, while rejecting the separatist temper that unchurches every assembly but its own and makes the purity of the gathered company a condition of Christ's presence in it.

The principle to recover is that God's work cannot be put down and men's work needs no persecuting. Gamaliel completes the argument: “But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it” (Act 5:39), lest you be found fighting against God. Christ says the same of every false growth, that “Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up” (Mat 15:13), and no magistrate is needed for the rooting. Meanwhile the duty of the believer is positive and unchanged: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25).

pos: n. (county town of Kent; where Kentish cloth-workers who read Tyndale were burnt under Mary)
etymology: From Old English Mægdestan, the maidens' stone; a meeting place by a stone.
biblical_def: Maidstone was the county town of a shire that read the Scriptures before most of England did. The Kentish Weald was full of cloth-workers and small farmers with Lollard grandparents and Flemish trading partners, and Tyndale's New Testament came up the Medway in bales of cloth; the county produced more recorded Protestants of humble rank in the 1530s than any other, and under Mary a series of them were burnt at Maidstone and Canterbury, among them Thomas Cole, a schoolmaster, and weavers and shearmen whose examinations survive. The dictionary records the town because the objection made against such people then is the objection still made, that unlettered men have no business interpreting Scripture. It was made against Christ Himself: “How knoweth this man letters, having never learned?” (Joh 7:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a craft as a trade, manual art, or employment requiring skill; prudent as cautious, wise in practical affairs; and a babe as an infant, and figuratively one of little learning.
webster_full: CRAFT, n. Art; ability; dexterity; also, trade; employment requiring skill or dexterity in manual labor.
PRUDENT, adj. [L. prudens.] Cautious; circumspect; practically wise; careful of the consequences of enterprises.
BABE, n. An infant; a young child of either sex; figuratively, one unskilled or of little learning.
OCCUPATION, n. [L. occupatio.] The principal business of one's life; vocation; trade; calling.
scriptures: Joh 7:15
And the Jews marvelled, saying, How knoweth this man letters, having never learned?
At that time Jesus answered and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes.
For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called:
Act 18:3
And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers.
corruption_summary: The Kentish county town, where cloth-workers who had read Tyndale were burnt under Mary; Tyndale came up the Medway in bales of cloth.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the clerical monopoly of interpretation, which Rome defended in law by forbidding vernacular Scripture to the laity and defends still in substance by reserving the authentic sense of the text to the magisterium. The dictionary grants the real danger it appeals to: untaught readers do err, and the remedy Scripture gives is teachers, not confiscation. The modern form of the monopoly is academic rather than clerical, and tells the ordinary believer that the text cannot be understood without a specialist's apparatus.

The principle to recover is that God has deliberately chosen the unlearned and the unimpressive to receive and carry His truth. Christ thanks His Father for the arrangement: “thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes” (Mat 11:25). Paul tells a congregation to look at itself, “how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called” (1Co 1:26). And the apostle to the Gentiles worked at a trade beside the men he taught, “for by their occupation they were tentmakers” (Act 18:3).

“for by their occupation they were tentmakers” (Act 18:3) — Thomas Cole, a schoolmaster, among them.

pos: n. (county town of Sussex; where seventeen Protestants were burnt in the High Street between 1555 and 1557)
etymology: From Old English hlāwas, the burial mounds; plural of hlāw, a mound or hill.
biblical_def: Lewes was the Sussex burning ground. Between June 1555 and June 1557, seventeen Protestants were burnt in front of the Star Inn in the High Street, the largest number at any single English site outside London and Canterbury; ten of them died together on 22 June 1557, among them Richard Woodman, an ironmaster of Warbleton who had been hunted for two years and was betrayed at last by his own brother. Their names are on a memorial above the town. The dictionary records Lewes because a company dying together is a particular form of this trial, and Scripture describes it: the martyrs under the altar are told to wait “until their fellowservants also and their brethren, that should be killed as they were, should be fulfilled” (Rev 6:11). The number is not accidental and it is not infinite.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fellowservant as one who has the same master; patience as the suffering of afflictions with a calm temper; and a witness as one who gives testimony.
webster_full: FELLOWSERVANT, n. One who has the same master.
PATIENCE, n. [L. patientia.] The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity, provocation or other evil, with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; also, one who gives testimony or evidence.
BESET, v.t. To surround; to enclose; to hem in; to waylay; to press on all sides.
scriptures: Rev 6:11

And white robes were given unto every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season, until their fellowservants also and their brethren, that should be killed as they were, should be fulfilled.
Heb 12:1

Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
Rom 8:18
For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.
Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus.
corruption_summary: Seventeen burnt in the High Street between 1555 and 1557, ten of them together on 22 June 1557.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The nearer error is the treatment of the Marian martyrs as a national or party monument rather than as Christians, which began almost at once: Foxe's book was chained in churches beside the Bible, and the martyrs became an argument for the English crown against Spain and Rome as much as a witness to the gospel. The dictionary records them as believers who died for a doctrine, and the doctrine, not the nation, is the point.

The principle to recover is that the roll of witnesses is a company we are joined to and are to run with. Hebrews makes them a reason for perseverance rather than for admiration, since we are “compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses” (Heb 12:1) and must therefore lay aside every weight. Paul sets the account straight for every such sufferer: “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom 8:18). And John names what is on display in them: “Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus” (Rev 14:12).

Greek hupomone (G5281) — patient endurance, perseverance; Revelation 14:12.

Greek euperistatos (G2139) — easily besetting, surrounding closely; Hebrews 12:1.

“compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses” (Heb 12:1) — Richard Woodman of Warbleton betrayed by his brother.
“Here is the patience of the saints: here are they that keep the commandments of God, and the faith of Jesus” (Rev 14:12) — seventeen in the High Street in two years.

pos: n. (port of the English west country; where Whitefield first preached in the open air to the Kingswood colliers in 1739)
etymology: From Old English Brycgstow, the place at the bridge; brycg, bridge, and stow, a place.
biblical_def: Bristol was England's second port and a town where preaching repeatedly broke out of its buildings. Hugh Latimer preached there in 1533 and was inhibited for it; the Broadmead congregation gathered in 1640 and became one of the oldest Baptist churches in the kingdom; Bristol Baptist College, the oldest in England, trained John Ryland and Robert Hall. In February 1739 George Whitefield, shut out of the city pulpits, went up to Kingswood and preached to the colliers in the open fields, to two hundred at first and within weeks to thousands; the coal dust on their faces was streaked with tears, and the white gutters, he said, showed him what was happening. He then persuaded John Wesley to do the same. The dictionary records the town because that decision rests on a commission with no buildings in it: “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a collier as a digger of coal, one who works in a coal mine; compassion as a suffering with another, pity; and a hedge as a fence formed with thorn or shrubs.
webster_full: COLLIER, n. A digger of coal; one who works in a coal mine; also, a coasting vessel employed in the coal trade.
COMPASSION, n. [L. compassio.] A suffering with another; painful sympathy; pity; commiseration.
HEDGE, n. A fence or boundary formed by a thick growth of thorn or other shrubs or small trees.
COMPEL, v.t. [L. compello.] To drive or urge with force, or irresistibly; to constrain; to oblige; to necessitate.
scriptures: And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
And the lord said unto the servant, Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled.
Mat 9:36
But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.
Testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: Latimer preached here in 1533; Whitefield first preached in the open air to the Kingswood colliers in February 1739.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the confinement of preaching to consecrated buildings and licensed occasions, which shut Whitefield out of the Bristol pulpits and which he answered by going to a field. The matching error belongs to the revival itself and the dictionary names it too: an irregular ministry that comes to despise the ordinary settled congregation, its discipline and its sacraments, and leaves converts attached to a preacher rather than gathered into a church. Whitefield was better on this than many who followed him, and Wesley worse.

The principle to recover is that the gospel is to be carried to men where they are, and that the preacher's motive is compassion rather than novelty. The parable sends the servant beyond the streets: “Go out into the highways and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled” (Luk 14:23). Christ's own reason for sending labourers is given plainly: seeing the multitudes, “he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd” (Mat 9:36). And the content stays the same in a field as in a pulpit, “repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ” (Act 20:21).

pos: n. (coal port of the English north-east; where John Knox preached as a licensed preacher from 1550 to 1553)
etymology: From the Norman castle built in 1080 on the Tyne; Old English nīwe, new, and castel.
biblical_def: Newcastle upon Tyne was where John Knox learned to preach to a congregation rather than to a garrison. Taken prisoner in the French galleys after the fall of St Andrews castle and released in 1549, he was licensed by the English council under Edward VI and sent to Berwick and then to Newcastle, where he served from 1550 to 1553, was made one of the king's six chaplains, and declined the bishopric of Rochester. He preached against the mass and against kneeling at communion, was heard by large congregations of the coal town, and fled abroad at Mary's accession. Those three years in an English border town are the whole of his settled parochial ministry. The dictionary records the town because the apostle's charge to a young minister describes exactly that kind of apprenticeship: “Meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them; that thy profiting may appear to all” (1Ti 4:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to meditate as to dwell on anything in thought, to contemplate; profiting as improvement, advancement in knowledge; and an evangelist as a preacher of the gospel.
webster_full: MEDITATE, v.i. [L. meditor.] To dwell on any thing in thought; to contemplate; to study; to turn or revolve any subject in the mind.
PROFITING, n. Improvement; advancement in knowledge or in anything valuable.
EVANGELIST, n. [Gr.] A writer of the history of Jesus Christ; also, a preacher of the gospel.
CHAPLAIN, n. An ecclesiastic who has the care of a chapel; a clergyman who officiates in the household of a prince or person of quality.
scriptures: Meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them; that thy profiting may appear to all.
Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.

And when he had found him, he brought him unto Antioch. And it came to pass, that a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people. And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch.
But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry.
corruption_summary: John Knox's charge from 1550 to 1553, the whole of his settled parish ministry; he declined the see of Rochester and fled at Mary's accession.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error nearer at hand is the modern impatience with apprenticeship, which puts untried men into prominent charges and then wonders at the wreckage. Knox had three years in an English coal town, under supervision, preaching twice on the Lord's day to people who had no particular reason to admire him, before he was anything at all; the Scotland of 1559 was served by what Newcastle had made of him. A second error belongs to Knox himself and the dictionary does not hide it: a temper that could not distinguish between the cause and his own vehemence, which cost him the Frankfurt congregation.

The principle to recover is that a minister is formed by continuance in a particular place and a particular doctrine. Paul joins the two objects of watchfulness and makes the outcome depend on both: “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them” (1Ti 4:16). The pattern at Antioch was a whole year of settled teaching before anything else is recorded of it, when “a whole year they assembled themselves with the church, and taught much people” (Act 11:26). And the charge is to finish what was begun: “do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry” (2Ti 4:5).
